sections.heading: Three numbers that are not the same: revenue, ARR, backlog
bullets: Revenue is what was billed this quarter. ARR (annualized run rate) is the last month's revenue × 12 — a snapshot of current pace, not a promise. Backlog (committed contract value) is everything customers have signed up to pay over multi-year terms
The three can tell wildly different stories at once: a neocloud can print $582M of quarterly revenue, $3B ARR, and $40B backlog — the backlog converts to revenue only as data centers energize
Take-or-pay contracts make backlog bankable: the customer owes the money whether or not it uses the capacity, so lenders treat signed backlog like a bond stream

Watch which number a company guides on. Guiding on ARR (a self-defined metric) is softer than guiding on revenue; beating your own ARR guide while missing revenue consensus is a recurring neocloud pattern

sections.heading: Contracted vs connected vs active power
bullets: Contracted power: land and utility commitments signed — the press-release number (a '5 GW target' means this)
Connected power: buildings finished and energized — the grid can feed them
Active power: IT equipment installed, running, and generating revenue — the only tier that pays for anything

The gaps between tiers measure execution risk in time: a company can hold 3.5 GW contracted with only ~170 MW active — a 20x buildout still to deliver, gated by transformers, permits, and construction crews
A useful productivity check: ARR per active MW (~$1M/MW is the current neocloud benchmark) links the power story to the revenue story

sections.heading: Full-stack cloud vs GPU landlord
bullets: A landlord rents raw GPU capacity under long contracts; a full-stack cloud adds the software above it — managed Kubernetes/Slurm orchestration, storage, observability, and an inference platform serving models per-token
Inference platforms sell tokens, not GPU-hours: customers hit an API for open models with SLAs, autoscaling, and fine-tuning — higher margin, stickier, and usage-based rather than committed
The stack is the defense against commoditization: when GPU scarcity fades and rental prices fall, the software layer and the developer relationships are what remain differentiated
Buying the stack is faster than building it: acquiring a search-API company, an inference-optimization team, and ML-tooling IP fills product gaps in quarters instead of years

sections.heading: The convertible-note treadmill
bullets: A convertible note is debt that can turn into shares at a set conversion price (typically 30-45% above today's stock) — cheap coupons now, dilution later if the stock rises
Growth neoclouds run ladders of converts: each new data-center wave is financed by a new tranche, and older tranches get 'exchanged' into shares to clear the way
The market's mood swings on this are violent: the same company can fall 14% in a day on dilution fears and recover 8% the next when it lands non-dilutive secured debt instead

Secured (asset-backed) debt is the graduation: once contracts with investment-grade customers exist, GPUs plus their contracted cash flows can collateralize loans at rates near SOFR+2.5% — replacing shareholder dilution with project finance
Off-balance-sheet items complete the picture: uncommenced leases and multi-year energy commitments can add $15B+ of obligations that never appear in the debt line

sections.heading: Anchor tenants: validation, concentration, and the boomerang
bullets: A hyperscaler signing a neocloud is powerful validation — it converts spare capacity into investment-grade backlog and unlocks debt markets
The price is concentration: two or three customers can become more than half of revenue, so any renegotiation, delay, or utilization shortfall at one anchor is a thesis-level event

The boomerang risk: today's anchor tenant is tomorrow's competitor — a hyperscaler renting third-party GPUs while building its own capacity may later sell its excess compute, competing directly with its former supplier
Chip-supplier circularity compounds it: when the GPU maker is also an equity investor in its customer's cloud, reported demand is partly self-referential

sections.heading: Power and permits: the new critical path
bullets: GPU delivery takes months; grid interconnection and air permits take years — execution risk has migrated from silicon to civil infrastructure

Behind-the-meter generation (on-site fuel cells, turbines) bypasses the interconnection queue; solid-oxide fuel cells have a second advantage — they avoid the Clean Air Act PSD review that gas turbines trigger, making them a permitting-speed play, not just a clean-power play
Local politics is a real schedule input: resident opposition, noise complaints, and unpermitted-work stop-orders can freeze a flagship site with billions of contracted revenue waiting on it

Waste heat is becoming a product: liquid-cooled AI factories in cold climates export recovered heat to district-heating networks — hundreds of GWh per year per gigawatt-site, turning a disposal problem into revenue and community goodwill

flashcards.q: Revenue, ARR, and backlog — which is a fact, which is a pace, which is a promise?
flashcards.a: Revenue is the fact (billed this quarter). ARR is the pace (last month × 12). Backlog is the promise (signed multi-year contract value) — it becomes revenue only as capacity energizes.

flashcards.q: A neocloud announces a '5 GW by year-end' target. What tier of power is that, and what tier pays the bills?
flashcards.a: Contracted power — land and utility commitments signed. Only active power (installed, running IT load) generates revenue; the contracted-to-active gap can be 20x and is the whole execution story.

flashcards.q: Why does take-or-pay structure matter more than contract size?
flashcards.a: Take-or-pay means the customer owes payment regardless of usage — it converts backlog into a bond-like stream that lenders will finance. A $10B usage-based contract is a hope; a $10B take-or-pay contract is collateral.

flashcards.q: What does an inference platform sell, and why is it strategically different from renting GPUs?
flashcards.a: Tokens through an API — model serving with SLAs, autoscaling, and fine-tuning. It's higher-margin, usage-based, and sticky, and it survives the moment GPU rental prices commoditize.

flashcards.q: How does a convertible note trade coupon for dilution?
flashcards.a: It pays a low coupon because holders get the right to convert into shares at a premium (30-45% above issue-day price). If the stock rises past the conversion price, the debt becomes new shares — the financing cost was deferred dilution.

flashcards.q: What marks a neocloud's 'graduation' in the debt markets?
flashcards.a: Its first secured, asset-backed facility: GPUs plus contracted cash flows from an investment-grade customer pledged as collateral at a tight spread (e.g., SOFR+250). Project finance replaces shareholder dilution.

flashcards.q: Where do billions of obligations hide outside the debt line?
flashcards.a: Uncommenced leases (signed but not yet started) and multi-year energy commitments. They bind future cash without appearing as debt — always add them to the leverage picture.

The hyperscaler that validates a neocloud today may later monetize its own excess GPUs — the customer becomes a competitor. Concentrated backlog carries this reversal risk on top of ordinary credit risk.

flashcards.q: Why can a stop-work order on one building threaten a $17B contract?
flashcards.a: Dedicated-capacity contracts deliver from specific sites on schedules. If permitting freezes the site (unpermitted fuel cells, LNG tanks, noise litigation), revenue timing slips even though demand, GPUs, and money are all in place.

flashcards.q: Why would a data center choose fuel cells over gas turbines even at higher cost?
flashcards.a: Permitting speed. Solid-oxide fuel cells avoid the Clean Air Act PSD review that combustion turbines trigger, and behind-the-meter generation skips the grid interconnection queue — schedule is worth more than the power-cost delta.

flashcards.q: How does a liquid-cooled AI factory heat a Finnish town?
flashcards.a: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling produces hot return water; a heat exchanger passes it into the district-heating network. At full scale a gigawatt-class site can export hundreds of GWh per year — waste heat becomes revenue.

flashcards.q: What is 'ARR per active MW' and what does it tell you?
flashcards.a: Annualized revenue divided by revenue-generating megawatts (~$1M/MW is the current benchmark). It links the power buildout to actual monetization — a falling ratio means capacity is outrunning demand or pricing.
